articles.title: The Sudan connection: Is Ethiopia at risk of a proxy war? - The Eastleigh Voice
articles.summary: The Sudan connection: Is Ethiopia at risk of a proxy war?  The Eastleigh Voice
articles.full_text:
Over the past week, three militias from a new alliance, led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), have been fighting the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) in northern Ethiopia.
            
                The heterogeneous alliance that calls itself the "Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival" brings together seven armed domestic groups that oppose Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.
            
                However, the ENDF has painted a picture of an alliance that extends far beyond Ethiopia's borders: Its commander-in-chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the TPLF.
            
                Sudan dismissed the allegation as "baseless." Its military government countered with accusations that Ethiopia was supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia that has been fighting Sudan's army for over three years.
            
                Eritrea said Ethiopia was attempting to shift responsibility for its own internal conflicts onto its neighbours. Cairo, meanwhile, issued a flat denial.
            
                A domestic conflict with 'external actors'
            
                Viewing developments in northern Ethiopia as a domestic affair is not the full picture, according to experts.
            
                "While it is primarily a domestic conflict, it certainly has a foreign policy dimension due to the many external actors directly or indirectly involved," said Susanne Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation.
            
                Stollreiter told DW that these actors have their own interests in the region — interests that could potentially be advanced by the conflict.
            
                "If this conflict escalates, I would even assume that it could truly lead to a kind of conflagration across the region, given the various conflict dynamics here in the Horn of Africa."
            
                Mirroring alliances between Ethiopia and Sudan
            
                Egypt and Sudan have long harboured grievances against Ethiopia because the source country of the Blue Nile dammed the river just before the border.
            
                Sudan has been caught up in a brutal civil war since April 2023. Both sides to the conflict — the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF militia — are believed to have ties to partners that are now fighting on opposing sides in Ethiopia.
            
                Sudanese greet army soldiers loyal to army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, in the Red Sea city of Port Sudan, on April 16, 2023. (AFP) 
                                    
                        Sudanese greet army soldiers loyal to army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, in the Red Sea city of Port Sudan, on April 16, 2023.(AFP)
                    
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
                    
                    
            
                On one hand, there's the Sudanese government and the TPLF, which was largely defeated in the 2020–22 Tigray War in Ethiopia. Many Tigrayan fighters went into exile in Sudan, where they organised as "Army 70" and fought alongside the SAF against the RSF.
            
                "They played quite an important role in the Sudan Armed Forces pushing back against the RSF in eastern Sudan and even into Khartoum. And then that relationship continued," said Magnus Taylor, Deputy Project Manager, Horn of Africa at the think tank International Crisis Group (ICG).
            
                "The issue that the federal government of Ethiopia has is that it appears that Sudan is in a kind of alignment or an alliance with one of the strongest opposition groups in the country."
            
                Tigrayan fighters in Sudan and training camp for Sudan militia in Ethiopia
            
                In May, the Sudanese government hosted high-ranking representatives of the TPLF and leaders of other Ethiopian groups that are critical of Abiy. Some of those groups are now part of the new seven-member alliance.
            
                On the other hand, there's Ethiopia's central government and the former Sudanese special unit, the RSF.
            
                In February, the news agency Reuters reported on a secret training camp for RSF fighters in the Ethiopian border region of Benishangul-Gumuz. According to the report, the United Arab Emirates provided instructors, funding, and logistical support — claims the UAE denied.
            
                Fighting between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigray fighters near the Sudan border has ended after nearly a day of clashes, raising fresh fears of renewed conflict. (Photo: Handout) 
                            
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
                    
                    
            
                The UAE is closely allied with Ethiopia and, despite denials, is considered the RSF's most important backer.
            
                Is Eritrea involved in the latest conflict?
            
                So far, there are no signs of direct involvement by the Sudanese army or the RSF in the conflict in Ethiopia. There is no evidence of Eritrea's role in the latest escalation either. But there's no shortage of wild speculation.
            
                Eritrea fought alongside Abiy's forces in the Tigray War, but the leaders of the two countries had had a falling out by the time the Pretoria peace agreement was signed in November 2022.
            
                Experts have long suggested that Eritrea — despite denials — is now supporting the TPLF. Distrust of Abiy runs deep, given his stated ambitions to secure Ethiopia access to the open sea — by force if necessary, such as by seizing the Eritrean port of Assab on the Red Sea.
            
                ICG analyst Magnus Taylor told DW that Eritrean involvement in the latest fighting is plausible.
            
                "I think the Eritreans have used the TPLF and other opposition groups to deter the perceived risk of Ethiopian aggression, whether that's for access to the port or other reasons," Taylor said.
            
                "Having a large physical presence within Tigray or within Afar even would be, I guess, a justification for the Ethiopians to carry out more extensive military operations on Eritrea. The Eritrean tactic is to deter military action, not to invite it."
            
                Asmara has strengthened relations with Cairo this year, and the United States has just let sanctions against Eritrea expire.
            
                Is there a risk of a wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa?
            
                The Horn of Africa borders the Gulf region in the north, which has lost stability due to the Iran war. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are also disrupting the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
            
                In Somalia, Al-Shabab is regaining ground, cooperating with the Houthis despite wide ideological differences.
            
                "These are important trade routes that are being disputed and fought over, and everyone is trying to profit from the unstable situation," Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation, said.
            
                "In this respect, it is no real coincidence that so many actors are now becoming particularly strong again, also because of the absence of the actors who were otherwise protective powers in the region."
            
                The US in particular, but also the Europeans tied down by Russia's war in Ukraine, have less of an eye on the Horn of Africa than before, Stollreiter said.
            
                Have Gulf powers taken sides in Ethiopia?
            
                The UAE and Saudi Arabia, which are accused of supporting different warring parties in Sudan and Yemen and have polarised the entire region in recent years, are all the more present.
            
                However, ICG's Magnus Taylor does not think that the situation in Ethiopia is at risk of escalating into a proxy war between the Gulf powers.
            
                "While the UAE is a strong backer of Addis Ababa, the Saudis are not strongly backing the TPLF or any other opposition group."
            
                Whether from the Arabian Peninsula, Sudan, or Eritrea — one week after the outbreak of war in Ethiopia, there are no clear signs that the internal conflict is becoming internationalised. However, in the unstable Horn of Africa, that risk is particularly high.

Airspace has been closed over part of Europe following a suspected drone sighting as Vladimir Putin appears to be continuing to test defences
NATO fighter jets have been scrambled following a suspected drone sighting over Lithuania with thousands of residents urged to find shelter.
Airspace has been closed over the Baltic state's capital Vilnius and a mobile phone alert sent to residents, telling them to find a safe place, according to local reports.
The suspected drone was detected entering Lithuania's airspace from key Russian-ally Belarus, which the country shares a south and eastern border with. It is thought it could be another example of Vladimir Putin testing NATO defences.
A senior official said fighter jets are investigating the sighting of the object which has not been "fully identified".
Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre, said the object resembles a drone on radar but did not rule out something less sinister, including a flock of birds.
Last month, an Italian figher jet stationed in the country was scrambled after a possible drone sighting which turned out to be birds.
Mr Vitkauskas said authorities received reports from residents of a "possible object outside the territory of Vilnius, moving towards Jonava". "But we cannot confirm this, because these are reports from residents," he told public service broadcaster LRT RADIO.
NATO countries in the Baltic have faced repeated drone incursions since Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The number of incidents have risen in recent months as countries along NATO's eastern flank warn of an increasing threat from Moscow.
A drone that entered Lithuanian airspace was shot down by NATO fighter jets last month. Authorities didn’t comment on the drone's origin or purpose, saying further investigation was needed after the incident on September 15, but two senior officials said the device was likely carrying explosives.
Officials in other NATO countries, including the UK, Germany, Denmark and Poland, have in recent weeks accused Russia of involvement in acts such as drone incursions, sabotage, arson and surveillance of defence facilities and in plans to use a drone carrying explosives to attack an airport.
Meanwhile Denmark said the same day as the Lithuanian drone was shot down, that one of its air force helicopters was fired on with flares as it was carrying out surveillance of a Russian frigate in the Baltic Sea.
Strikes close to NATO territory showed Putin’s “desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in response. Rutte has pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance’s own defences along its long eastern border with Russia and its ally Belarus,

articles.title: Cyber Attackers are targeting Critical Infrastructure. Here’s how States can fight back. - Cybersecurity Insiders
articles.summary: Cyber Attackers are targeting Critical Infrastructure. Here’s how States can fight back.  Cybersecurity Insiders
articles.full_text:
Today’s cyber environment is dynamic and increasingly perilous. Artificial Intelligence is intensifying the speed, sophistication and complexity of cyber threats across the United States. Risks to the critical infrastructure we all rely on, including water supplies, hospitals, energy networks and transportation systems, are growing every day. In this rapidly evolving cybersecurity landscape, state governments across the country play a crucial role in protecting our critical infrastructure.
According to a new report from General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT) and the National Association of State Chief Information Officers, almost 90% of state CIOs now rank cyberattacks on critical infrastructure as a big concern. This is especially true for smaller municipalities and special districts that are particularly vulnerable to malicious actors.
States are also navigating a wide variety of challenges, including deep uncertainty about federal funding, escalating cyber‑physical threats, fragmented authority and gaps in capabilities across local governments and special districts. Given this scenario, building trust and collaborative relationships has become as crucial as legal authority, and innovative governance models are propelling progress.
Unified, statewide cyber defense strategies are emerging as powerful tools for enhancing infrastructure security. Many states now embed critical infrastructure protections within their overall cybersecurity frameworks.
New York’s recent funding initiative for water systems and Utah’s shared cybersecurity services, covering most local entities, are prime examples. Oregon is assembling diverse partners to fortify sector-wide defenses, while some states rely on voluntary programs and service offerings instead of mandates.
Small communities and specialized districts remain the most vulnerable, often lacking cyber-trained staff and operating legacy systems. To bridge these gaps, states are providing hands-on support like education, incident response services, risk management and security assessments.
For example, Kansas has widened access to state cyber services, and Minnesota has enacted executive orders to mobilize support during incidents. The most popular offerings include expert guidance, governance partnerships, financial support, coordinated responses and shared solutions.
Funding uncertainty is a persistent challenge. Most state CIO budgets cover executive branch cybersecurity, but few extend support to local agencies and districts. The possibility of reduced federal funding could threaten progress, making legislative and targeted grants increasingly important. Continued national investment remains essential for safeguarding vulnerable infrastructure.
Operational technology and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems present pressing risks, especially for water, health and transit services, due to their reliance on older equipment, remote connections and unclear responsibility boundaries.
States are shifting toward regular assessments and coordinated oversight to reduce cyber risks. Recent cyber incidents targeting water utilities have prompted federal guidance and underscored the need for stronger cyber protection.
Looking forward, states must act decisively to protect our critical infrastructure. Below are three low-cost, realistic steps that authorities across a state can take:
1. Map high-risk systems, prepare for advanced threats like AI-driven attacks, reinforce partnerships and clarify oversight frameworks. Determine which systems would have the most real-world impact if targeted and focus resources there. Ensure you know the right points of contact of vendors, partners, third-party contractors, and state and federal partners before an incident occurs.
2. Promote best practices such as cyber hygiene, incident reporting and expanding support services. Change all default passwords and choose a long and strong pass phrase instead. Run a 60-minute incident response tabletop exercise with your frontline operators to discuss the basics: what triggers outreach and communication? How do communications flow within and outside of the organization? How do you reach external government resources (i.e.: State & Federal Partners, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), FBI, etc.)? Prioritize patching based on operational risk in your environment. And ensure manual mode remains an option for operators.
3. Cultivate independent funding sources at the state level, when possible, to ensure cyber resilience, while maintaining sustained federal funding. Take maximum advantage of free resources, such as CISA best practices, Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) membership and open-source threat feeds. Describe cyber risks in mission and business impact language when advocating for funding. Translating cyber risks into plain language about impact to citizens and customers helps ensure that risk-based decisions are fully understood.
As cyber risks mount, proactive state leadership and cross-sector cooperation will be vital to protecting essential services and the public’s well-being. Critical infrastructure cybersecurity directly shapes Americans’ safety, security and daily lives. From citizens to government officials to frontline operational technology and IT operators to cybersecurity professionals, we all must understand what is at stake and do our part. It is imperative that we get this right.

articles.title: Africa and the UN Security Council: Is the Permanent Seat Really Worth the Hassle? - Nigerian Voice
articles.summary: Africa and the UN Security Council: Is the Permanent Seat Really Worth the Hassle?  Nigerian Voice
articles.full_text:
The 81st United Nations General Assembly had almost everything we have come to expect from a gathering of world leaders. While conflict and humanitarian crises dominated much of the conversation, the event also featured dramatic walkouts and intense debates over artificial intelligence. Amid these discussions, U.S. President Donald Trump's push to rename the technology "Super Intelligence" (SI) marks only the latest in a series of rebranding efforts pursued by his administration.
And then there was the rather less diplomatic sight of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa apparently scrolling through Instagram Reels while Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğanwas speaking. But beneath all these familiar dramas was a question that deserves a closer look: the continuing push to reform the United Nations Security Council.
Africa's demand for permanent representation on the Security Council is hardly new. In 2005, the African Union adopted the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration, setting out what became known as the Common African Position on Security Council reform. Africa called for no fewer than two permanent seats, with the same privileges attached to existing permanent members, including the veto for as long as the veto itself remains. It also called for additional five non-permanent seats for Africa.
In 2008, the General Assembly launched the intergovernmental negotiations process on Security Council reform, yet twenty-one years later, the demand is still on the table. In fact, the issue has received renewed attention. At the opening of the 81st General Assembly, the call was once again placed firmly on the international agenda, with the UN Secretary-General describing Africa's exclusion from permanent membership as increasingly difficult to justify. Echoing this sentiment, African leaders like William Ruto, Julius Maada Bio and Kashim Shettima united to demand immediate permanent seats, forcefully arguing that the world of 2026 cannot remain captive to a distribution of power drawn up in 1945.
What exactly is Africa fighting for?
The United Nations Security Council is the body primarily responsible for maintaining international peace and security. It has 15 members: five permanent members—the United States, China, Russia, France and the United Kingdom—and ten non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. Unlike the ten elected members, the permanent five possess veto power, meaning that a negative vote from any one of them can prevent the adoption of a substantive resolution. The Council can impose sanctions, establish peacekeeping operations and, in certain circumstances, authorise the use of force.
This is where Africa's argument becomes understandable. Africa is home to 54 United Nations member states and more than 1.5 billion people. Its population is expected to reach roughly 2.5 billion by 2050, meaning that more than a quarter of the world's population could be African. The continent is also deeply affected by the decisions of the Security Council, particularly on questions of armed conflict, sanctions, peacekeeping and international intervention. For instance, in 2025, the Council adopted 44 resolutions, including 24 under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, which covers measures such as sanctions and authorisations for the use of force. Eighteen of those 24 Chapter VII resolutions concerned Africa.
The argument, therefore, is straightforward: a continent that is so heavily affected by international peace and security decisions should have a permanent role in making them.
Who exactly represents Africa?
Nigeria would almost certainly enter the conversation. Its population, economic weight, diplomatic history, peacekeeping record and influence in West Africa provide a substantial basis for its claim. South Africa would also be difficult to ignore, given its economic and diplomatic influence, its experience in multilateral institutions and its previous service on the Security Council. Egypt brings its demographic and strategic importance, its position linking Africa and the Middle East and its long diplomatic history. Ghana, meanwhile, has its own credentials, including its diplomatic tradition, peacekeeping contribution and relatively strong democratic institutions. Other countries such as Algeria, Ethiopia and Kenya would also have reasons to enter the conversation.
As it turns out, Africa's external demand for representation may be easier to articulate than Africa's internal agreement on who should exercise that representation.
But Would a Permanent Seat Actually Solve Africa's Problems?
The case for African representation is compelling. But representation and transformation are two different things. A permanent seat would give Africa greater influence over decisions on international peace and security, but it would not, by itself, resolve the problems that continue to shape everyday life across the continent.
Take insecurity, for example. Africa continues to deal with devastating conflicts and political instability. The Security Council already spends considerable attention on African conflicts and Africa remains central to the Council's peace and security agenda. A permanent African member could certainly give the continent a stronger voice in how these crises are discussed and addressed. But it would not automatically stop a war, defeat an insurgency or prevent a military coup. Those challenges also depend on the strength of national institutions, regional cooperation, accountable leadership and the willingness of governments to address the conditions that allow conflict to persist.
The same applies to poverty and unemployment. Africa is home to some of the world's fastest-growing populations, but economic growth has not always translated into enough jobs or significant improvements in living standards. The World Bank estimates that about 464 million people in the region were still living in extreme poverty in 2024, while the region continues to struggle to create enough productive employment for its growing young population. A permanent seat in New York cannot build a factory, reform a broken education system or put a young person into a decent job. Those are largely questions of domestic policy, institutions, investment and economic management.
There is also a more uncomfortable problem: governance. A permanent seat cannot manufacture strong institutions. It cannot make governments more accountable to their citizens, strengthen courts, eliminate corruption or make public officials more responsive. These are problems that Africans must confront largely through domestic and regional political action. A country can have a seat at the world's most powerful diplomatic table and still struggle to provide basic services to its own citizens.
None of this means that Africa should abandon its demand for a permanent seat. That would be a false choice. International representation matters, particularly for a continent whose countries are deeply affected by decisions made within the Security Council but have no permanent member of their own.Perhaps, therefore, the more important question is whether we see the seat as an instrument of African interests or as an achievement in itself.
Abdulhameed Oladele Lukman writes on governance, youth participation, and democratic development. He ca n be reached via aolukman05@gmail.com .

articles.title: Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books - The Guardian
articles.summary: Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books  The GuardianCulture Under Fire: Ukraine’s Fight Against Russia’s Campaign of Erasure  Council on Foreign Relations (CFR)Erasing history: Putin’s ‘genocidal’ attacks on Ukrainian culture  The TimesTaras Shevchenko Museum damaged in Russian attack on Kyiv  UkrinformJOHNSTON: Russia is committing genocide in Ukraine  Kingston Whig
articles.full_text:
On a Saturday morning in August, Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, was at his headquarters in Kharkiv – the eastern Ukrainian city that, along with Kyiv, is the centre of the country’s publishing and printing industry. Built 15 years ago on the site of a former bread factory, the footprint of the premises is about 10,000 sq metres (107,640ft). Books were stacked 12 metres high on rank after rank of shelves.
Kruglov, along with five senior colleagues, were on the warehouse floor to discuss the approaching school year. The warehouse was holding 628,000 new schoolbooks. “It was the high season of distribution,” he said, “so we were checking all our processes: how to do it more successfully, how to do it in time.”
The meeting was scheduled for 11am. But a couple of moments after it began, there came “the sound of an explosion, and almost simultaneously I saw a huge fire”, said Kruglov. The impact was about 30 metres from where the staff were gathered, and, as colleagues set about trying to put out the flames, “there came a second strike and I understood that there could be a third, and a fourth, so we started to evacuate”.
The munitions used in the attack were jet-powered Shaheds, a recent and insidious escalation of Russian drone technology, faster and harder to intercept than their predecessors. These are the weapons that have been lately terrorising Kyiv during daylight hours, ploughing into the National Academy of Sciences and a working medical clinic in the past week.
“Fifty people were on shift that day,” said Kruglov of the warehouse strike, “and I don’t know how to explain how nobody was injured.”
The combination of an explosion, jet fuel and a warehouse full of paper was catastrophic. None of the books could be salvaged and 8m were destroyed. It took firefighters a week to bring the flames under control.
Several weeks on, smoke still rose from parts of the warehouse. The roof seemed on the verge of collapse, metal beams listing alarmingly, twisted out of shape by the heat.
Shafts of sunlight slanted through the damaged roof, illuminating the catastrophe. The smell was terrible, clinging to clothes and hair. As far as the eye could see, the wreckage of books lay in mounds.
In some places, engulfed by the firefighters’ water, they had dissolved into a thick, stinking, mud-like slurry. In others, they were charred at the edges but recognisable as what they once were: children’s picturebooks illustrated with animals and flowers, geography textbooks, young-adult fiction. Others were nothing but swollen millefeuilles of blackened pages that flaked away to the touch.
A couple of editorial staff, visiting the wreckage for the first time since the attack, looked shaken as they recognised fragments of books they had written or edited. “When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it’s an awful feeling,” said Kruglov, a trim, bald, blue-eyed man in his early 60s.
Those 8m books represented more than 85% of Ranok’s total stock, he said. In the main branch of Ranok’s own Knyholand bookstore in Kyiv, the display still looked cheerful and dense in late September – but, predicted Kruglov, there will be shortages this autumn when the books instore run low and there is nothing to replace them.
In total, this summer, 13m Ukrainian books have been destroyed by Russian missiles or drones – a third, estimates the government, of all books printed in Ukraine this year.
Books, literature, culture and language are not peripheral to Russia’s war on Ukraine – they are bound up in it. The full-scale invasion in February 2022 was prompted, at least in part, by Vladimir Putin’s conviction that Ukraine and Russia have no true separate cultural identity.
Kruglov said he was sure his warehouse full of Ukrainian-language, Ukraine-produced books had been deliberately targeted. “It is nowhere near any military facilities and everyone knows it is a book warehouse,” he said.
Bohdana Laiuk, a Ukrainian deputy minister for culture, who works on literature and publishing, takes a slightly different view: the recent attacks on books should not be seen in isolation, but as part of the invaders’ recent campaign of attacking warehouses, depots and fulfilment centres of any kind. “They cannot occupy Kyiv,” she said. “So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us – and books are part of everyday life.”
But books are also part of language, and language is part of identity and, often, nationhood. Books are, said Laiuk, certainly considered important by the Russians invaders. “When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do – and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions – is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them,” she said.
Until 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market was Russian-language titles – most imported from Russia, some published in Ukraine.
The dominance of Russian publishing had a long history. Its seeds lay in 19th-century decrees under the tsars against publishing in Ukrainian and continued through the Soviets’ promotion of Russian as the language of aspiration, education and culture. Ukrainian writers were purged and Ukrainian literature left in the shadows, shut out from a canon that lionised the Russian novel.
After Ukraine’s independence in 1991, the idea of a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel that tackled modern social issues was so unthinkable that publishers initially suggested to Oksana Zabuzhko that her 1996 novel Fieldwork in Ukrainian Sex be published in Russian translation. She insisted it was published in the language it was written. It became a bestseller, paving the road for waves of contemporary Ukrainian literature.
Laiuk characterised the dominance of Russian book imports as a kind of colonialism. “It should be compared to how Russians invested in Ukrainian media outlets, Ukrainian TV channels, Ukrainian newspapers and magazines.” It was a conscious policy, she argued. “This is how Russians think: when they arrive on tanks, everything will be ready for them because they already have this information space.”
But in 2022, Ukrainian booksellers abruptly stopped selling Russian imports, in line with the rupture of all commercial ties between the countries. At the same time, swathes of the Ukrainian population switched their day-to-day language from Russian to Ukrainian.
They switched reading matter, too, and Ukraine’s publishers fed the appetite with new editions of classic Ukrainian literature from the 1920s, poetry, translations, and new Ukrainian writing. The country’s publishers may publish Russian-language books, as long as at least half their titles are in Ukrainian; in practice the social barriers to doing so, at the moment, would be prohibitive. (Death and the Penguin author Andrey Kurkov, for example, writes his novels in Russian, but they are published only in Ukrainian translation; he writes nonfiction and children’s books in Ukrainian.)
“People began to understand that the Russians came here to kill people simply because they were Ukrainian,” Laiuk told me in 2023. “So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are.”
Oleksiy Erinchak opened the first of his chain of Ukrainian-only bookstores, Sens, in 2021. In 2024, while the city was under fire, he opened a second, in a huge building on Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s grandest boulevard, to which he has recently added a third floor, with an expansive events space. He has another branch in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk and he has just opened a fourth, in a former cinema in Lviv.
“When you go to a bookstore like Sens,” said Laiuk, “you feel that you have dignity. You have the right to buy a new book and to choose which one you like. And when you have drones above your head, it gives so much space, inner space in your heart and soul, and in your mind.”
The rapid expansion of Sens is a symptom of something unlikely: a Ukrainian publishing boom amid a full-scale invasion of the country. And now, that boom is threatened by the force and frequency of Russian attacks.
Kateryna and Artem Sova started their imprint in 2023, in the thick of the new Ukrainian publishing boom. By then Artem had been in the army for nearly a year and Kateryna was several months pregnant, living in her hometown of Kremenchuk, on the River Dnipro in central Ukraine. It was their dream: they had both worked in bookstores and at arts festivals for years. Part of the point for Artem was to keep some chink of his old self alive. “I realised,” he said, speaking in Zaporizhzhia during a break from his military duties, “that I was detached from everything I love.”
They began with Lonely City, a nonfiction work about art and the experience of urban isolation, by the British author Olivia Laing. They had loved it since they read it a decade ago, and were bemused it was not already translated. They wrote to Laing’s agent asking whether they could acquire the rights.
“We tried to explain why this book is important for Ukrainians now, and to me personally,” Artem said, recalling. “This experience of being lonely is kind of universal, but it has been multiplied because a lot of people went into the army, and there are so many displaced people in Ukraine: separated couples, destroyed lives.”
Laing, to their surprise, agreed: only then did they actually go through the legal process of setting up the company. articles.title: Pakistan and Afghanistan used to be allies but they're edging towards all-out war - DW.com
articles.summary: Pakistan and Afghanistan used to be allies but they're edging towards all-out war  DW.comPakistan launches deadly air strikes on Afghanistan  BBCPakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan kill 10 civilians, Kabul and UN say  AP NewsWhy Pakistan Turned on the Taliban (and Vice Versa)  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs MagazineWhy Afghanistan is becoming a pressure point for Pakistan’s Middle East ambitions  Middle East Monitor
articles.full_text:
On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan. The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots.
These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm.
The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces. On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the deaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan.
Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed.
TTP and Taliban: A complex relationship
The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state.
Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor.
Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult.
"Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC.
The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence.
"The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere."
This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked.
Difficult borders
There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan.
The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan.
So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity.
"Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created.
In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban.
"While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes.
Pakistan exerts pressure
Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners.
Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon. Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory.
So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan.
An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban.
The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied.
"It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition."
Significant escalation
This is turning the dispute over the TTP into a larger conflict in which both sides accuse each other of supporting armed groups from the other's territory.
British think tank Chatham House speaks of a significant escalation compared to previous border skirmishes. Worryingly, a conflict over armed groups and border incidents is turning into a direct confrontation between the two nation states.
Ruttig believes that it would be possible to contain the spiraling violence if both sides return to negotiations.
"If both sides were willing to return to the negotiating table — perhaps with international mediation —there would be ways to contain the conflict and, above all, to protect the civilian population on both sides," he argues.
In a late September commentary in Pakistani weekly magazine The Friday Times, Pakistani analyst Saqib Ali Khan advocates for several things that could ease the tensions. That includes a reliable channel between Islamabad and Kabul, a separate approach for armed groups and greater involvement of the population along the border.
The conflict, he argues, is not merely a dispute between two governments but also a security, border, economic and regional conflict.
"Along those lines, there would have to be a shift in perspective on both sides," Schetter concludes.
In the long term, greater economic integration is also needed, he adds, so that Pakistan and Afghanistan do not define their relationship solely through security and power issues.
This story was originally published in German.

articles.title: With complicity of media and Democrats, Trump prepares major escalation of Iran war - World Socialist Web Site
articles.summary: With complicity of media and Democrats, Trump prepares major escalation of Iran war  World Socialist Web Site
articles.full_text:
The events of the past week leave no doubt that the Trump administration, with the complicity of the entire US political establishment, is preparing a major escalation of the Iran war. Having failed to achieve its objectives through a massive bombardment and then a blockade of the country, the White House is preparing a new and desperate gambit, potentially involving the deployment of ground troops or even the use of nuclear weapons.
The greatest danger is the chasm between the scale of what is being prepared and the public’s awareness of it. One month before the 2026 midterm elections, Trump’s conspiracy to escalate the war is being greeted with a wall of silence by the US media—which devoted just minutes to the war in this weekend’s Sunday talk shows—and by the Democratic Party, which has done nothing to alert the public to the renewed onslaught against Iran that the administration is preparing.
On September 22, US President Donald Trump threatened in his speech before the United Nations to “annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly.” His threat followed a secret White House meeting, reported by the journalist Seymour Hersh on June 10, at which Trump spoke “about a nuclear option that could perhaps bring a quicker end to the war.”
These threats cannot be dismissed as bluster. Trump is the president of the United States and has already killed thousands of people in the months-long bombardment of Iran. The forces now converging on the Persian Gulf give him the means to carry out his threats. Nothing would be more dangerous than complacency.
After seven months of war, US imperialism has failed to achieve its aims of dominating the Strait of Hormuz, militarily defeating Iran and overthrowing its government. The administration is improvising, desperately seeking a way out of the political disaster the war has produced. But its improvisation is driven by the logic of events. American imperialism cannot accept defeat in the Persian Gulf, and each failure becomes the basis for an ever-greater escalation.
Last week, the Wall Street Journal and the Associated Press reported that the White House had sent a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East. The USS Theodore Roosevelt left San Diego on September 27, followed the next day by the amphibious assault ship USS Makin Island with about 2,200 Marines. They will join the carrier USS George Washington and more than 50,000 US troops deployed across the region.
Trump “has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms,” the Journal reported September 25. He was briefed in August on options including “sending in ground forces to seize Iranian islands near Hormuz,” the Journal reported last month.
The deployment of amphibious assault ships along with thousands of Marines is particularly ominous. They are the means of seizing territory, and the next phase of the war may include landings on the islands near Hormuz, at the Kharg Island oil terminal or at Iran’s nuclear sites.
The administration’s top national security officials met Friday at Camp David, the presidential retreat, “to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen,” Axios reported that night. The last similar meeting, Axios noted, was in June 2025, just days before Israel and then the United States attacked Iran. The new US military deployments targeting Iran parallels a renewed offensive by Saudi Arabia, supported by the United States, in Yemen.
The Pentagon confirmed Sunday that all US bombers at Britain’s Fairford air base, used for strikes on Iran, had been flown back to the United States. The withdrawal followed British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s claim on September 30 that Iran “played a part” in an alleged plot against the base. The unproven allegation provides a ready-made pretext for escalation.
The war against Iran is part of a broader global offensive by US imperialism, centrally targeting Russia and China. Significantly, the plans to expand the Iran war accompany a sharp intensification of NATO’s war on Russia in Ukraine, which threatens at any moment to erupt into direct warfare between nuclear-armed states.
Each president since the 1979 Iranian revolution, Democratic and Republican, has worked to bring Iran back under American domination. Trump’s war against Iran is the latest stage of a 35-year offensive to subjugate the Middle East and Central Asia: the Gulf War of 1991, the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, the destruction of Libya, the proxy war in Syria and Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Amid overwhelming popular opposition to the war and the ensuing surge in the cost of living, particularly of energy, the Democratic Party is expected to make significant gains on November 3. It is determined, however, to ensure that any electoral repudiation of Trump does not lead to a let-up in the drive by US imperialism in the Middle East.
The Democrats’ policy is to “win this war,” as Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona said on CNN on September 30. Senator Chris Coons of Delaware, the senior Democrat on Pentagon appropriations, said on CNN Thursday that Trump needed to “come up with a plan that can work and that doesn’t leave Iran permanently in control of the Strait of Hormuz.” Democratic Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, a former Navy pilot, faulted Trump on ABC’s “This Week” on September 27, saying, “We can’t leave the Strait in the hands of the Iranians.”
None of the party’s congressional leaders has called for halting the new deployment. Rather, 58 House Democrats, among them former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, voted with Republicans on September 16 for a bill expanding Trump’s tariff powers against Russia and extending the sanctions on Iran. The party is running 67 congressional candidates “with a national security background, more than double the number who ran in any of the last four elections,” the World Socialist Web Site reported in a series that began last week. After the elections, the Democrats intend to work with Trump to escalate war throughout the world.
Opposition to the war is overwhelming, but the media, the Democratic Party and the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) are working to prevent its translation into action. The DSA plays a critical role in demobilizing antiwar sentiment. Jacobin, the magazine aligned with it, has not reported Trump’s plans to attack Iran after the election, and neither Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont nor Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, a DSA member, has issued a statement on them.
The escalation of war abroad is accompanied by an assault on the working class at home. The price surge triggered by the war has led to a disastrous reduction in workers’ living standards. Diesel has risen from $3.76 a gallon the day before the war began to $6.34 on Sunday, according to AAA.
Trump said April 1 that, with the country “fighting wars,” it was “not possible for us to take care of day care, Medicaid, Medicare—all these individual things.” The White House has asked Congress for a $1.5 trillion military budget for fiscal 2027, a 42 percent increase, while cutting nondefense spending by 10 percent. The war budget and the attack on social programs are a single class policy.
The struggle against war and its disastrous economic consequences cannot be subordinated to the Democratic Party, which is fully committed to the predatory aims of US imperialism. Ending the war against Iran and halting the global eruption of American imperialism requires the independent mobilization of the working class on the basis of a socialist program, seeking to unite the struggle against war with the defense of jobs and living standards.

articles.title: Between Entrapment and Abandonment: The Mecca Pact Faces Its First Serious Test - RealClearDefense
articles.summary: Between Entrapment and Abandonment: The Mecca Pact Faces Its First Serious Test  RealClearDefenseTurkey says Mecca pact committee to meet in Riyadh on October 5  ReutersPakistan suggests talking to Houthis as Riyadh weighs military options  The Arab WeeklySaudi Arabia not to compromise on security as Houthis choose ‘chaos’: MBS  Al JazeeraAs Saudi Arabia steps up war against Houthis, Pakistan set to play support role  South China Morning Post
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye made an unusually sweeping promise to one another when they signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on August 7: an armed attack on one would be treated as an attack on all three. The agreement seeks to strengthen collective deterrence by confronting potential adversaries with the combined power of three of the Muslim world’s most consequential states.
Less than two months later, that promise is facing its first serious test. Houthi missiles and drones have repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia. Pakistan has carried out air and drone strikes inside Afghanistan amid escalating cross-border violence. And Türkiye’s increasingly adversarial relationship with Israel has taken on a dangerous military dimension in Syria.
These developments expose a dilemma built into the pact from the start. Make the guarantee broad enough to deter, and the three countries risk being drawn into wars arising from threats they do not share. Limit it enough to preserve strategic autonomy, and the pact risks losing the credibility that gives collective defense its deterrent power.
Alliance theory has long grappled with this tension. Glenn Snyder described alliances as caught between abandonment and entrapment: states seek commitments strong enough to ensure that allies will defend them, but not so expansive that they are dragged into conflicts in which their own vital interests are not at stake. Deterrence makes this balancing act harder. As Thomas Schelling argued, a commitment deters only when an adversary believes it will be honored. A military alliance therefore derives much of its value from the credibility of its promise to act together.
For the Mecca pact, therein lies the dilemma: the more unequivocal the promise, the greater the risk of entrapment; the more discretion members preserve, the greater the risk that adversaries doubt the promise altogether.
The difficulty is magnified because the three states operate in largely distinct threat environments. Pakistan’s overriding external concern remains India, its nuclear-armed rival to the east. The two countries fought major wars in 1947–48, 1965, and 1971; clashed in Kargil in 1999; and have experienced repeated military crises since, including their brief but intense confrontation in May 2025. Pakistan also faces militant violence and chronic insecurity along its western frontier. Saudi Arabia confronts Iran, the Houthis, and broader Gulf security challenges. Türkiye faces Kurdish armed groups, instability in Syria, Black Sea security concerns, NATO obligations, and an increasingly difficult relationship with Israel.
Such differences are not unusual among allies. NATO members have long disagreed over particular threats and regions. The harder problem for the Mecca pact is that its broad defense guarantee attempts to bridge three substantially different security environments. One member’s most important crisis may therefore create expectations of military support in a conflict the other two have powerful reasons to avoid.
The Houthi campaign provides the clearest indication yet of how this dilemma operates in practice. Since the Houthis declared a naval blockade of the kingdom in July, their missile and drone attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy sites, and shipping. On September 19, Saudi air defenses intercepted a missile aimed at Riyadh. A week later, they intercepted two drones heading toward Riyadh and two ballistic missiles aimed at Khamis Mushait.
The alliance has begun responding. Türkiye’s foreign minister said on September 19 that Ankara was ready to help meet Saudi Arabia’s military needs, particularly on technical issues. On September 25, the Saudi, Pakistani, and Turkish defense chiefs and chiefs of general staff met in Riyadh under the Mecca agreement. They reviewed threats facing the kingdom and discussed intelligence cooperation, military coordination, and integration of capabilities. They also pledged to “immediately begin” translating the pact’s commitments into effective military cooperation.
But there is a meaningful difference between helping Saudi Arabia defend itself and entering another Yemen war. Pakistan and Türkiye may be willing to provide intelligence, air-defense capabilities, technical assistance, logistics, or other defensive support. Direct combat against the Houthis is another matter, and neither government has publicly announced plans to join it.
Pakistan demonstrated something similar under its bilateral defense relationship with Saudi Arabia during this year’s Iran war. Reuters reported in May that Islamabad had deployed roughly 8,000 troops, a fighter squadron, two drone squadrons, and an HQ-9 air-defense system to the kingdom, with personnel primarily serving in advisory and training roles. Pakistan, meanwhile, mediated between Washington and Tehran rather than joining offensive operations against Iran.
This is precisely where Snyder’s dilemma interacts with Schelling’s. Limited involvement reduces the danger of entrapment. Yet each limitation also communicates something about what “an attack against all” means in practice. If attacks on Saudi territory produce intelligence cooperation, air defense, and technical assistance but not direct military action against the attacker, allies and adversaries alike learn something about the boundaries of the guarantee.
Pakistan’s escalating confrontation with Afghanistan exposes the same problem from the opposite direction. Islamabad struck targets in eastern Afghanistan on September 21 and, three days later, said it had struck ten locations it described as launch and storage sites for drones used against Pakistan. Kabul rejected Pakistan’s account and said four civilians were killed.
There is no evidence that Pakistan has invoked the Mecca agreement over Afghanistan, nor that Saudi Arabia or Türkiye has been asked to participate. Pakistan is helping to operationalize collective defense in support of Saudi Arabia while confronting a serious security challenge of its own. If the confrontation with Afghanistan escalates, Riyadh and Ankara could eventually face the same question Islamabad now confronts over Saudi Arabia: how far does collective defense extend when an ally’s security crisis grows out of a complicated cross-border conflict? Supporting Pakistan’s territorial defense is one thing; becoming implicated in a Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict is another.
Türkiye presents a potentially more dangerous version of the dilemma. Its relationship with Israel has deteriorated sharply, and Syria has emerged as a possible military flashpoint. In mid-August, Israel struck Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase, saying Damascus was on the verge of allowing Turkish troops to deploy there. Syria’s foreign minister said no Turkish base was planned, and Türkiye’s defense ministry denied that a Turkish delegation was present at the site. Washington has said it is working to establish a deconfliction mechanism among Israel, Syria, and Türkiye, but the episode shows how competing Turkish and Israeli objectives in Syria could produce a military confrontation.
A direct Turkish-Israeli confrontation would pose difficult choices for Riyadh and Islamabad. Türkiye also belongs to NATO, so an attack on Turkish territory could, depending on the circumstances, generate consultations and political pressures under two alliance frameworks. NATO’s Article 5 obliges allies to assist an attacked member but leaves each ally discretion over the action it considers necessary, including whether to use armed force. The Mecca pact could therefore face both the problem of entangling its members in one another’s conflicts and the complications of overlapping collective-defense commitments.
Pakistan’s nuclear arsenal raises the stakes further. Nothing publicly available establishes that Islamabad has formally extended a nuclear guarantee to Saudi Arabia or Türkiye, and assuming otherwise would be a mistake. Yet deterrence operates partly through perception. Pakistan is one of nine nuclear-armed states and the pact’s only nuclear-armed member. Its arsenal was developed primarily to deter India, not to underwrite contingencies in the Gulf or the Levant. Will adversaries nevertheless perceive it as standing somewhere behind the promise that an attack on one will be treated as an attack on all?
If they do, deterrence could strengthen – but so could the consequences of entrapment. A conventional crisis involving Saudi Arabia or Türkiye could acquire a nuclear shadow none of the three governments intended.
These cases point to the same structural trade-off. A broad guarantee gives potential adversaries more reason to hesitate but expands the range of conflicts capable of implicating all three allies. A narrow guarantee protects strategic autonomy but reveals where collective action stops. The Mecca pact therefore becomes most effective as a deterrent precisely when it becomes most dangerous as an alliance.
Here the effort to avoid entrapment creates a second danger: a credibility trap. Limited involvement allows a state to avoid an unwanted war, but each limitation reveals something about how far the alliance is prepared to go. Allies may fear abandonment while adversaries learn where collective defense stops. What begins as useful strategic ambiguity can gradually become a map of the pact’s boundaries.
The three governments appear to recognize the problem. At the inaugural meeting of the pact’s Strategic Political and Defence Committee in Istanbul on August 31, their foreign and defense ministers and senior military leaders agreed to further institutionalize cooperation, establish a permanent secretariat in Saudi Arabia, strengthen defense capabilities, and ensure the “credibility and effectiveness” of collective deterrence and defense. They also stressed de-escalation and restraint. The September 25 meeting of their military chiefs suggests this process is moving from institutional design toward operational coordination

articles.title: Key Biden aide Brett McGurk on Hamas, Iran, Saudi Arabia and why U.S. nearly took "draconian measures" against Israel - CBS News
articles.summary: Key Biden aide Brett McGurk on Hamas, Iran, Saudi Arabia and why U.S. nearly took "draconian measures" against Israel  CBS News‘Ready to Blow His Stack’: How Biden Nearly Cut Off Netanyahu Over Gaza  nytimes.comBiden Reportedly Considered Cutting Arms to Israel  YahooHow Biden Averted a War With Iran  The AtlanticTranscript: Brett McGurk on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Oct. 4, 2026  CBS News
articles.full_text:
President Joe Biden was on the verge of taking "draconian measures" after an Israeli military drone strike killed in the Gaza Strip in April 2024, but U.S. intelligence that Iran was about to launch an "unprecedented" prevented Biden from moving forward, according to Brett McGurk, a top Middle East adviser to four presidents.
In an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" taped Thursday, McGurk described Biden as "fed up" with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war in Gaza.
"At that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces … I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel," he said, adding that cutting off U.S. weapons to Israel "was very much on the table."
The U.S. and its Arab and European partners helped protect Israel from the Iranian attack, which McGurk said included 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones and 30 cruise missiles that were "all launched to land at the same time."
In his new memoir titled "Brink," which is set to be published Tuesday, McGurk recalled a tense conversation between Biden and Netanyahu around that time in which the U.S. leader warned the prime minister he could end the weapons supply. At the time, the Israeli government said it believed there were more than 130 hostages in Gaza and around 34,000 Gazan deaths, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Ministry of Health.
"You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal," McGurk quotes Biden as saying.
In McGurk's interview with CBS News, the longtime foreign policy aide recounted the Biden administration's initial reaction to Hamas' Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel, its handling of Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza, the efforts to secure an Israel-Hamas ceasefire and hostage release deal, the role of Iran and — starting years earlier — a long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
McGurk is no longer working with the Bidens and is currently a CNN contributor.
McGurk: "If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis"
Biden's handling of the Israel-Hamas war has drawn years of scrutiny — including from within his own party. During the 2024 presidential campaign, the administration faced to stop military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
The U.S. is the largest weapons supplier to Israel, and provides billions in aid. A of Israel's conduct found that it was "reasonable to assess" that Israeli security forces have used U.S.-made weapons in ways "inconsistent with" international humanitarian law obligations. Casualties in Gaza, "including high levels of civilian casualties," raised "substantial questions as to whether the IDF is using" U.S.-made weapons "effectively in all cases," the report said.
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen in November 2024 that Biden didn't use U.S. leverage effectively, arguing he sent Israel "more bombs and more money" after Netaynahu disregarded his requests, and pointed to U.S. laws blocking arms shipments to military units that violated human rights.
Since then, debates over the future of U.S.-Israel relations have . Some of the criticism that the Biden administration was not strong enough in its response to Israeli actions in Gaza has been directed at McGurk, who was the White House National Security Council's coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa and one of his most influential advisers.
McGurk noted that the Biden administration did to Israel, including 2,000-pound bombs but never instituted a weapons halt. He believes some of the calls to go further may not have been effective.
"Israel also has one of the largest arms industries in the world, so the idea that had Biden gone further on a step on that course, it would have stopped the war, I just think the record does not support that," McGurk said.
McGurk also argued that exerting too much public pressure on Israel could have hardened Hamas' stance, ultimately setting back the negotiations to end the war in Gaza and release the hostages.
"I come back to the question: How do you end this crisis?" he said. "And I think the record shows: If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis, it's going to make it worse."
At the same time as the Israel-Hamas war, attacks on U.S. forces by Iranian-backed proxy groups surged. McGurk pushed Biden to punish Iran in an effort to deter the attacks, and expressed some frustration with Biden administration colleagues who were wary of striking Iranian officials in response.
What would've happened if Iran "made a dash" toward weapons-grade uranium
McGurk said part of Biden's goal was to prevent the outbreak of a broader regional war. Meanwhile, between Iran and Israel continued.
In December 2024, McGurk traveled to Israel with national security adviser Jake Sullivan as they worked toward a deal with Hamas to release the remaining Israeli hostages.
During the visit, according to McGurk, Netanyahu talked about taking out nuclear sites in Iran, including at Fordow, a facility built inside a mountain that processed and stored highly enriched uranium. Fordow was one of the three Iranian nuclear sites that President Trump ordered to be bombed , eight months before the Trump administration and Israeli forces launched a wider war against Iran.
McGurk said the Biden administration was concerned in late 2024 that Iran "might make a dash" toward making weapons-grade uranium, and officials were open to carrying out strikes if there were evidence obtained that showed Iran was making a bomb. Netanyahu urged the US not to wait for that step. Iran had been building up a stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium, which is a short step from the material required to build a bomb.
"We actually had a principals committee meeting — that's everybody around the table — what would we do if we see that?" McGurk said. "And as I recall, unanimity on: We would do the strike in Fordow. We didn't see that. We sent a message to Iran, don't even think about it. But yet Netanyahu was clearly contemplating that."

U.S. saw no "warning or indicator" of Oct. 7 attack
The circumstances leading up to the Oct. 7 attack have drawn renewed attention in recent weeks, as The New York Times, The Atlantic and the Israeli newspaper Haaretz report on warnings that officials in Egypt and the United Arab Emirates allegedly delivered to Israel that Hamas was planning a major attack. Netanyahu has strongly denied that there were any warnings, but his opponents in Israel's election later this month have expressed outrage.
CBS has confirmed via a former US official and a diplomatic source that Emirati Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan, President of the UAE, did share a warning with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu in the weeks leading up to the attack. The UAE had learned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major attack but did not have specific intelligence such as a date, time or location.
McGurk told CBS News the U.S. had no intelligence that could have warned about Hamas' Oct. 7 attack.
"We did not have anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator," he said. "No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator."
But he said Israel should launch an official inquiry that probes its own security establishment and political leadership, much like the U.S. did after the 9/11 attacks.
"I think they had an assumption that was deeply ingrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any scale like this," McGurk said. "I think that was a false assumption in their system, a failure of imagination, and it was tragic."
McGurk on the Biden-MBS fist bump: "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand"
Hours before the Oct. 7 2023 attack, McGurk said he met with the Saudi Arabian Ambassador to the U.S., Princess Reema Bandar, to discuss a different issue — a potential pathway for Israel and Saudi Arabia to normalize relations.

"I believe that we are at the cusp of an even more dramatic breakthrough: an historic peace with Saudi Arabia," Netanyahu said.
The idea of Saudi Arabia establishing formal diplomatic ties with Israel had been floated to McGurk by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman nearly two years earlier, in January 2021, shortly after Biden took office, McGurk said, a deal that would have included a pathway to a Palestinian peace agreement.
